question: Xi Jinping out before 2027?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if China's General Secretary of the Communist Party, Xi Jinping, is removed from power for any length of time between July 3, 2025, and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping will be considered removed from power if he announces his resignation from his role as General Secretary, or is otherwise dismissed, detained, disqualified, or otherwise loses his position or is prevented from fulfilling his duties as General Secretary within this market's timeframe.

The primary resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.

eventMetadata.context_description: Xi Jinping's entrenched position as paramount leader of the Chinese Communist Party, reinforced by the 2018 removal of presidential term limits and successive purges of military and political figures through mid-2026, underpins trader consensus that he will remain in office through the end of 2026. Recent developments, including the ouster of senior generals such as Zhang Youxia and Politburo members, have been read as measures that further centralize authority rather than erode it, while Xi continues to direct diplomacy, economic planning, and preparations for the 21st Party Congress scheduled for late 2027. With no designated successor elevated to the Politburo Standing Committee and elite promotions emphasizing loyalty, the probability of an abrupt leadership change before 2027 stays low in the absence of verifiable institutional challenges. Only low-probability events such as a sudden health crisis or an unforeseen elite revolt could still shift the outcome.

eventMetadata.context_description: Trader sentiment for the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee shows a fragmented field, with Gavin Newsom, Jon Ossoff, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez holding slim leads as no candidate has consolidated broad support. Early-cycle dynamics include competing coalitions of progressives and moderates, varying name recognition from Senate and gubernatorial roles, and positioning after recent electoral setbacks.
